title: Differential Amplifiers
intro: Differential circuits dominate analog design because they reject common-mode noise and distortion. This chapter (Razavi, Chapter 4) goes from the idea of differential signalling to the differential pair, its large- and small-signal behaviour, its response to common-mode inputs, its loads, and the Gilbert cell.

items: Single-ended and differential operation: common-mode level, swing, and immunity to coupled noise and supply noise.
The basic differential pair: current steering, input common-mode range, the large-signal law $I_{D1} - I_{D2} = f(V_{in1} - V_{in2})$, and small-signal gain by superposition or the half circuit.
The degenerated pair: a wider linear range in exchange for gain.
Common-mode response: common-mode gain, mismatch-driven common-mode-to-differential conversion, and CMRR.
MOS loads: diode-connected, current-source, auxiliary current sources and the cascode pair.
The Gilbert cell: variable-gain amplifier, multiplier and mixer.

blocks.caption: Differential gain of a resistively loaded pair at equilibrium.
Input difference that steers the whole tail current to one side.
Common-mode rejection limited by a transconductance mismatch and the tail resistance.

blocks.text: Work through the pages in order: the half-circuit idea from the differential-pair page is used on every later page and in the next chapter's active-mirror analysis.
